notes.title: Deeper Analysis of Bar Graphs
notes.content: At Level 2, questions are not just direct reading. You must compare values, calculate percentage changes, ratios, and averages. First scan the entire graph, then read the question carefully, and finally perform calculations.

notes.title: Double and Multiple Bar Graphs
notes.content: When two or more bars are shown for each category (such as different years), make a small rough table to organize the data. This reduces confusion and calculation errors.

notes.title: Percentage Change Concept
notes.content: Percentage Increase equals (Increase divided by Original value) multiplied by 100. Percentage Decrease equals (Decrease divided by Original value) multiplied by 100. Always divide by the original value, not the new value.

notes.title: Ratio and Comparison
notes.content: To compare two values like 300 and 450, write them as a ratio and simplify. 300 to 450 becomes 2 to 3 after dividing both by 150.

notes.title: Average Based Questions
notes.content: If data for several years is given, first find the total sum, then divide by the number of years. Arrange numbers properly before adding.

notes.title: Combined Data Questions
notes.content: Sometimes you need to combine two categories before comparing. For example, total sales of Product A and B together compared with Product C.

notes.title: Advanced Common Mistakes
notes.content: Using the wrong base value for percentage. Ignoring one category while adding totals. Confusing years in double bar graphs. Not checking units carefully.

notes.title: Strategic Approach
notes.content: Solve direct questions first. Use approximation when numbers are large. Keep rough work organized. Avoid re-reading the entire graph for every question.

tricks.title: Fast Percentage Increase Trick
tricks.explanation: Find the difference first, then compare it with 10% of the original value to estimate quickly.
tricks.example: From 400 to 500, increase is 100. 10% of 400 is 40. Since 100 is 2.5 times 40, increase is 25%.

tricks.title: Quick Ratio Simplification
tricks.explanation: Try dividing both numbers by 5, 10, or 25 first to simplify faster.

tricks.title: Smart Average Method
tricks.explanation: If numbers increase evenly, the average is the middle value.

tricks.title: Approximation for Large Numbers
tricks.explanation: Round off numbers to nearest tens or hundreds before calculating percentage.
tricks.example: 498 can be treated as 500 for quick estimation.

tricks.title: Difference Comparison Trick
tricks.explanation: Instead of calculating full percentage for two cases, compare absolute differences first.
tricks.example: Increase from 300 to 450 is 150, while 400 to 500 is 100. First case has higher growth.

tricks.title: Total Percentage Method
tricks.explanation: To find share of a category, first calculate total, then divide.
tricks.example: If total sales are 1000 and Product A is 250, share is 25%.

tricks.title: Double Bar Fast Handling
tricks.explanation: Calculate yearly differences first, then compare trends.
tricks.example: If Year 1 difference is 60 and Year 2 difference is 90, Year 2 shows bigger gap.

tricks.title: Option Elimination Strategy
tricks.explanation: If answer choices are far apart, estimate first and remove clearly wrong options.
tricks.example: If answer is around 48%, remove 10% and 90% options immediately.
